title: Facing injustice
hookLine: standing up for what is right, peacefully first
tomorrow: someone comments 'go back home' under Simran's photo. now what?

lines: A FRESHMAN IN A NAVY PATKA.
HER FIRST THOUGHT: GET IN HIS FACE.
cards: The bus stop, early, and the freshman in the navy patka is staring at his shoes. His name is Arjan; his family moved here this year. A junior keeps flicking the knot on top of his head while two friends film and laugh.

Simran sees it from across the street, and her first thought is the loud one: drop the backpack, get in his face. She crosses. She stands right next to Arjan, holds up her own phone, and says, very calmly: stop.
I'm recording too, and the vice principal gets both videos. The laughing stops. Then the bus pulls up, and nobody knows yet what happens next.

teach.h: GURU NANAK NAMES WHAT HE SAW.
teach.b: What Simran did has an old shape. Guru Nanak lived through an invasion. When Babur's army swept into the Punjab, the Guru didn't stay quiet.
In hymns now in the Guru Granth Sahib, he names what he saw. On Ang 360 he even turns to God and asks, in paraphrase: there was so much beating that people cried out; did you feel no pain?

teach.h: TRUTH, AT THE TIME OF TRUTH.
teach.b: On Ang 722 he says, again in paraphrase: Nanak speaks the word of truth, and will tell the truth at the time of truth. So standing up starts with naming the wrong, out loud, even to power.
Here's the detail worth telling a friend tonight: that hymn about an invasion is addressed to Bhai Lalo, a carpenter in Sikh tradition. Truth about kings, sent to a working man.

Generations later, Guru Gobind Singh writes the Zafarnama, a letter to the emperor Aurangzeb. One line in it says, in paraphrase, that when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword.
Look at the order in that sentence.
Every other means comes first. Force is the last door, never the first one.

teach.h: SEE IT, STAND BESIDE, NAME IT.
teach.b: So facing injustice has a sequence: see it, stand beside the person it's hurting, name it plainly, and make sure the people who can act will hear.

how: Sikhs often point to the Gurus as people who named injustice openly, and some Sikh groups today speak up for people being harassed, through words, schools and the courts.

o: seeing a wrong and naming it out loud, peacefully first
getting even with anyone who hurts your own people
staying calm and saying nothing so it all blows over

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: a carpenter a truth hymn is sent to
the sword only after every other means
stood beside him and named it

s: the Sikh way is to answer cruelty with a fight
the Zafarnama puts every other means first; force is the last door, never the first.
Guru Nanak named an invasion's cruelty in his own hymns
on Ang 360 he even asks God, in paraphrase, did you feel no pain?
speaking up only counts if you win the argument
Guru Nanak's line is to tell the truth at the time of truth; winning isn't the measure.

games.q: a group chat is piling a cruel nickname on a classmate who isn't in it. going by today, what's the first move?
o: post one plain line, 'stop, that's not okay,' and tell someone who can act.
screenshot it all and post it publicly to shame them right back.
stay out of it for now, and speak up only if it gets physical.
games.why: see it, stand beside the person, name it plainly, let the right people hear: the sequence Guru Nanak's hymns and the Zafarnama point to. peacefully first.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've watched happen that wasn't fair, at school, at work, or online. Say out loud, in one plain sentence, what you'd say next time, something like: stop, that's not okay.
Say it again, slower and calmer each time, until it sounds like your own voice.

wordCard.voice: Facing injustice. Seeing a wrong, standing beside the person it's hurting, and naming it out loud, peacefully first.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sach, truth. Guru Nanak will tell the truth at the time of truth (Ang 722).

carryVoice: Hold onto this: stand up, with words first, the way Guru Nanak named what he saw. Day 1723, and Arjan wasn't alone at the bus stop.

sources.ref: Ang 360, Asa, Guru Nanak (Babarvani: 'eti maar pai kurlaane tain ki dard na aaia'), paraphrased
Ang 722-723, Tilang, Guru Nanak (addressed to Lalo: 'sach ki baani Nanak aakhai, sach sunaaisi sach ki bela'), paraphrased
Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh (the couplet on taking up the sword when all other means have failed), paraphrased
